items.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: we did those things behind Rebecca [Kilgore], it’s lovely

ctx.x: When were you first able to use your arranging skills?

Well I’d done some things mostly with doing things for singers, you know Maxine Sullivan and just arranging stuff behind her. Because with singers it’s nice to have a little organized backing like we did tonight, we did those things behind Rebecca [Kilgore], it’s lovely. You know it makes all the difference because it gives it a nice little showcase setting for a singer. And I do like singers. A lot of musicians don’t like singers, but I like

it because you’re hearing the lyrics, and it’s good to work, I think there’s a very healthy cabaret scene. That’s one thing — I mean the jazz scene to me is not particularly, say interesting, it’s not, it doesn’t interest me much today, I mean what’s going on in contemporary ways, which may sound a bit fuddy duddy to you, but I don’t believe that anything that’s thirty, forty years old is particularly old. Perhaps we Europeans, we have a different time concept. But you know to me Jerome Kern and these melodies…

items.title: Rebecca Kilgore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997
items.q: Well I heard you last night. I guess you were singing with Keith [Ingham].

ctx.x: Sure. Because Dave and I have a rapport after having worked together for so long, like five and a half years, and I know a lot of obscure songs. That’s kind of what I gravitate to. I don’t do a lot of standards, which sometimes is a disadvantage. So he and I do these obscure songs and we kind of have these arrangements worked out, and I thought oh boy, this will be fun to pull out some of our strange material and kind of bring something new and different. And well that’s out the window, because a lot of these…

Well I heard you last night. I guess you were singing with Keith [Ingham]. And it got to the end of the tune and you did something that was very musical to do — and I’m not even sure I can describe it, but it just had something to do with when you were going to tag, that you made it obvious, you sang an obvious note so that he knew, okay tag. And then when you got to the very end you just held this note out and let him, and he did kind of his [scats]. But you just held that thing out there, and it sounded like it…

Well I think that a good guide is to keep it as simple as possible. I’m not going to add a whole bunch of embellishments. I’ll just kind of keep to a very simple concept and let the pianist fill in the blanks.
